newsitem.title: GERMANY: China's Hong Kong chief says HK to be trade bridge.
newsitem.headline: China's Hong Kong chief says HK to be trade bridge.

text.p: Beijing's Hong Kong policy chief said on Monday that Hong Kong would continue to be a bridge to the West for China, with guaranteed human rights and press freedom, after it returns to Chinese sovereignty on July 1.

Lu Ping met German industrialists and foreign policy experts in Bonn at the start of an eight-day trip to Germany and Austria, the first of a series of visits to reassure Western investors about the handover.
Lu said China would encourage Western businesses to use Hong Kong as an entry gate to mainland China.

"Its main contribution will be that it plays the role of a bridge for China to enter western markets and for the West to enter the mainland Chinese market," he told a news conference after the meeting. "(Hong Kong) will contribute greatly to our opening-up policy and so there will be no change," he added.
Lu sought to allay fears that Beijing would clamp down on freedoms when it took over.

He said the Bill of Rights which guarantees civil rights in the British colony would be altered only to remove passages which give it supremacy over the colony's other laws and to make it subordinate to the Basic Law or constitution.
"The substance of the Bill of Rights will remain," he said.
Lu said guaranteed press freedoms would also remain, although he suggested it was doubtful whether Hong Kong media would be allowed to advocate secession from China.
"'Advocacy' is different from press freedom, it's a kind of action," he said. "But what kind of 'advocacy' is illegal -- that will be decided by the Hong Kong courts."
He said other countries including the United States had laws limiting the freedom of the press to advocate secession.

Lu also denied that the troops of the People's Liberation Army to be stationed in Hong Kong would be used for internal security, and said their contingent would be smaller than the current British garrison.

Ekkehard Goetting, the South China and Hong Kong delegate for the German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), said German businesses, like those in Britain, the United States and Japan, were very relaxed about the handover.
He said more than three-quarters of relevant businesses polled by the DIHT said they expected to do as much or more trade with Hong Kong after the handover, and practically none expected a decline.
"The vast, vast, vast majority consider Hong Kong as the key entry point for their China business... The vast majority would like to increase their own activities.

"They see in the long term, roughtly five years from now, their business increasing, prospects in China improving, other regional centres and markets, for example Vietnam, being served out of Hong Kong. In essence they are saying that Hong Kong's oustanding position.. will remain unchanged or even improve."
